About: The Electromagnetic Wave

Source

Concept
Slide from radio to γ-ray: wavelength collapses by fourteen orders of magnitude while E/B never moves off c.
Serves
Structure of a plane EM wave (E ⊥ B ⊥ k, in phase); B = E/c; wavelength × frequency = c across the spectrum; intensity depends on E0, not on f.
Inquiry
Before touching frequency, predict what happens to the magnetic-arrow amplitude as you sweep radio → X-ray.
Misconception
“E and B take turns like a pendulum swapping kinetic energy for potential.” They do not — they peak together, and their energy shares are equal at every instant.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict — from radio to γ-ray

The frequency slider runs from radio (106 Hz) to γ-ray (1020 Hz) — fourteen orders of magnitude — with the electric amplitude E0 held fixed. What does the magnetic amplitude B0 do as f climbs?

2 · Sweep it — watch the wavelength collapse

Drag the frequency slider left to right. The wavelength readout falls from hundreds of metres (radio) through micrometres (infrared) and nanometres (visible) to picometres (γ-ray).

The view keeps ~2.6 wavelengths in frame at every setting, so read the collapse from the λ readout and the per-λ scale under the z-axis, not from the picture.

The one ratio: E0/B0 = c ≈ 3.00 × 108 m/s — every frequency, every amplitude, every band.

3 · The energy split

“E and B take turns storing energy — one peaks while the other is zero, like a pendulum swapping KE for PE.” True or false?

4 · Explore — what E0 controls

Now try the electric amplitude slider. The blue arrows grow — and so do the pink ones, in lockstep, because B0 = E0/c. The wavelength does NOT move: amplitude is not frequency.

Doubling E0 quadruples the intensity (I = ½ε0c E02) — check the I readout at 10 V/m and again at 20 V/m. Frequency plays no role in intensity at all.

The Electromagnetic Wave

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A plane electromagnetic wave travels along z, with an electric field E and a magnetic field B at right angles to each other. The frequency slider moves it across the whole spectrum, from radio to γ-ray, and the sim reads out what each setting means.

What you'll learn

  • How the wavelength depends on the frequency, across fourteen decades.
  • How the field amplitudes and the intensity depend on the frequency and on E₀.
  • How the electric and magnetic parts of the wave are arranged along z, and how they share the energy.
The three directions, and the spectrum the frequency slider sweeps.

What's on screen

  • E, the electric field: blue arrows and curve, standing up from the z axis.
  • B, the magnetic field: pink arrows and curve, in the perpendicular plane, drawn ×c so they are visible beside E.
  • E × B: the amber arrow for the direction of travel, and the marker on the spectrum strip.
  • Readouts: wavelength λ, magnetic amplitude B₀, intensity I and the ratio E₀/B₀.
See itLook at the opening setting, 10¹⁴ Hz. Watch for: the blue and pink arrows, the amber travel arrow, and the marker on the strip reading infrared.

03

The wavelength is c divided by f

Every electromagnetic wave in vacuum travels at the same speed, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. In one period 1/f it moves one wavelength, so

λ = c / f
λ is the distance between successive peaks.

Each factor of 10 in f shrinks λ by a factor of 10. Across the slider's fourteen decades, λ runs from hundreds of metres down to a few picometres.

fBandλ
10⁶ Hzradio300 m
10¹⁰ Hzmicrowave30.0 mm
10¹⁴ Hzinfrared3.00 µm
5.01 × 10¹⁴ Hzvisible598.2 nm
10¹⁸ HzX-ray299.8 pm
10²⁰ Hzγ-ray3.00 pm

The picture always fits about 2.6 wavelengths, so read λ from the readout and from the "per λ" label under the z axis.

The band edges on the strip are the sim's own round numbers. Other books draw them a little differently.

See itSet f to 10⁶ Hz, the radio end. Watch for: λ reading 300 m and the z label saying 300 m per λ, while the picture still shows about 2.6 waves.
04

The magnetic amplitude is E₀ divided by c

Faraday's law ties the two fields of a travelling wave together. A wave E₀ cos(kz − ωt) needs B₀ω = E₀k, so the peak values obey

E₀ / B₀ = ω / k = c   so   B₀ = E₀ / c
E₀ in V/m, B₀ in T, and c in m/s.

The frequency f appears nowhere in this relation, so sweeping f leaves B₀ alone. Only E₀ sets it. The speed itself comes from c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀): with ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m this gives 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s.

E₀B₀ = E₀/c
10 V/m3.34 × 10⁻⁸ T
20 V/m6.67 × 10⁻⁸ T
40 V/m1.33 × 10⁻⁷ T

B₀ is tiny in SI units, which is why the sim draws B ×c. The ratio readout always shows c.

See itSet f to 10¹⁸ Hz with E₀ = 20 V/m, then drag f. Watch for: B₀ at 6.67 × 10⁻⁸ T and E₀/B₀ at 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s, while the band and λ change.
05

E and B peak together in a travelling wave

Both fields carry the same phase kz − ωt, so they cross zero at the same z and peak at the same z, at every moment:

E = E₀ cos(kz − ωt)    B = (E₀/c) cos(kz − ωt)
E, B and z are mutually perpendicular, and E × B points along +z.

The energy follows. Using B = E/c and c² = 1/(ε₀μ₀), the magnetic energy density equals the electric one:

uB = B²/(2μ₀) = ½ ε₀ E² = uE
Each is half of the total u = ε₀E², at every point and every instant.

So energy does not swap back and forth between the fields in a travelling wave. A quarter-cycle offset between E and B belongs to a standing wave.

See itWatch the opening wave run. Watch for: the blue and pink arrows shrinking to zero at the same z together, and the caption "E and B are in phase".
06

The intensity depends on E₀ and not on f

The intensity I is the average power the wave carries through each square metre facing it. The average energy density is ½ε₀E₀², and that energy moves at c:

I = ½ ε₀ c E₀²
I in W/m², with ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m.

Frequency does not appear, so I is the same at 10⁶ Hz and at 10²⁰ Hz for the same E₀. Doubling E₀ quadruples I.

E₀I
10 V/m1.33 × 10⁻¹ W/m²
20 V/m5.31 × 10⁻¹ W/m²
40 V/m2.12 W/m²
See itSet E₀ = 10 V/m, then drag E₀ up to 20. Watch for: I at 1.33 × 10⁻¹ W/m² first, then 5.31 × 10⁻¹, and the wavelength not moving.
See itNow set f to 10²⁰ Hz at E₀ = 20 V/m. Watch for: I still at 5.31 × 10⁻¹ W/m², the value it had at 10¹⁴ Hz.
07

Where it matters

  • Radio and microwaves. FM radio at 100 MHz has λ ≈ 3 m, and a microwave oven at 2.45 GHz has λ ≈ 12 cm. Both come from λ = c/f.
  • Visible light. The eye responds from about 430 to 750 THz, which is λ from about 700 nm down to 400 nm, a sliver of the strip.
  • X-rays. At 10¹⁸ Hz, λ ≈ 0.3 nm, about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why crystals diffract X-rays.
Go deeper: sunlight as a plane wave

Sunlight at the Earth carries about 1.36 kW/m². Treated as one plane wave, I = ½ε₀cE₀² gives E₀ ≈ 1.0 kV/m and B₀ = E₀/c ≈ 3.4 µT. That is far beyond this sim's 40 V/m, but the same two formulas apply.

08

Summary

In one line. An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has wavelength λ = c/f, and this sim sweeps f from radio to γ-ray while you read λ, B₀ and I.

Key points

  • λ = c/f: each factor of 10 in f shrinks λ by a factor of 10.
  • E₀/B₀ = c at every frequency, so B₀ = E₀/c depends on E₀ alone.
  • E and B are in phase, and their energy densities are equal at every instant.
  • I = ½ε₀cE₀² depends on E₀, not on f.

Common mix-ups

  • "E and B take turns, like kinetic and potential energy." They peak together, with equal energy densities.
  • "A shorter wavelength means a smaller magnetic field." λ only spaces the peaks. Their height is E₀/c.
  • "A higher frequency means a higher intensity." At a fixed E₀, I is the same at every frequency.

Things to try on your own

  • Drag f until the band reads visible, and read λ.
  • Set E₀ to 27.5 V/m and check that I reads about 1 W/m² at any f.
  • At three frequencies, divide E₀ by B₀ yourself and compare with the ratio readout.
